newsitem.title: USA: New Minnesota tobacco law challenged in court.
newsitem.headline: New Minnesota tobacco law challenged in court.

text.p: R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. has sued Minnesota to block a new state law requiring tobacco companies to identify and then disclose the levels of lead and other toxic substances in their cigarettes.
The company filed the suit on Tuesday in U.S. District Court in St. Paul, arguing that the Federal Cigarette Labeling and Advertising Act does not require disclosure of ingredients.
The federal statute is the one that requires warnings on packages and in advertising that cigarettes are harmful to health.

The Minnesota law, signed last Friday by Gov. Arne Carlson, requires tobacco companies to identify and then begin disclosing the presence of five substances in their products -- ammonia, arsenic, cadmium, formaldehyde and lead.
"They must have a lot to hide," Minnesota Atty. Gen. Hubert Humphrey III said, referring to tobacco companies.
"Why else would they be fighting so hard to keep the public from learning the hazardous substances in cigarettes?
"We don't let people put cadmium in ink or paint. It's too hazardous," he added.
"What other business in the history of America has the unmitigated gall to say that its customers have no right to know if the products they're ingesting contain arsenic?"

In its suit Reynolds admitted the company adds certain ingredients to help give cigarettes their distinctive characteristics, but it said the Minnesota law was unconstitutional because it would force the company to disclose trade secrets.
